posts.author: Martin
posts.content_md:
> **glajciorz:** Tell me please, which step is the most critical - I guess bromide+dye bath timing - since it determines grain size. But which else ?

If the layer is too soft, it may become difficult to get an even silver loading or avoid layer damage.

I guess the single most difficulty with the diffusion method is getting consistent results. Subtle changes might have huge effects.

> Could I harden emulsion using formaldehyde (I also have chrome alum, but I'd like to know which one will be better) ?

I assume formaldehyde is OK – as long as you can remove it prior to the sensitizing baths – otherwise you may risk fogging.

> After exposure I'd like to develop in metol-acorbate, use Fe-EDTA bleach and iodine treatment. What deveploper and bleach do you recommend/use with DIY plates ?

If the layer is sufficiently hardened, ascorbate developers are fine. For softer emulsions Neutol (hydroquinone/phenidone) or CW-C2 like developers were more forgiving.

> One more - did you try coating non-glass materials (for example laser transparencies) using diffusion method ?

Yes, I've tried to apply the diffusion method to several kinds of of inkjet materials. The ones I've seen, turned out to be poorly water resistant though.

Coating on plastic substrates is said to require subbing layers and the plastic materials to be plasma treated etc. However, we may have found another method that allows gelatin coatings on a great many substrates (PMMA, PC, PE, TAC etc.) without any of the above mentioned requirements. More tests are under way.

posts.content_md:
Hi.

2 weeks ago I started making my own plates using Jeff's diffusion method. The system works fine.

Could you tell me about your observations on making your own plates ?

I used photographic grade gelatin (15% solution), 6% AgNO3 solution (kept in the darkness at room temperature). KBr+dye solution was kept in the darkness at 4 deg.C without traces of air in the container. Ag loading lasted 4' (1ml/plate), KBr bath was 4' too.

All solutions were made using DI water.

2,5x2" glass plates were presoaked overnight in 10% KOH/isopropyl alcohol solution, rinsed in tap water, rinsed in DI water, wiped dry with towel paper, cleanroom tissue and blown with canned air.

Here's what I know or what seems to me now and please correct me if I'm wrong:

- formaldehyde solution seems to be better hardener than alum - since formaldehyde is a gas and it escapes from gelatin while curing at 60 deg. C. (?) No further rinsing in DI water is needed. I've made test holograms on rinsed and not-rinsed plates. I've seen no difference.

- I tried to make gelatine-AgNO3 solution (to eliminate Ag loading step) by adding 3g of AgNO3 to 50 ml gelatine solution (to achieve c.a. 6% AgNO3 concentration) heated to 50 deg.C. Solution became turbid after adding AgNO3 (traces of halides in gelatine ?). Glass plates were pre-warmed to 40 deg.C. After courtain-coating 3 samples were soaked in formaldehyde, 3 were left unsoaked. All samples were dried at 30 deg.C during 5h in darkness. Hardened samples looked brownish (AgNO3 decomposition ?) After curing all samples were placed in KBr+dye bath for 4'. Unhardened gelatin went away from the glass. 

Hardened and sensitized gelatin seems to have some photosensitivity, but I was not able to make them completely black after exposing to white light and developing (what was possible with plates made with unaltered diffusion method). Maybe lowering concentration of formaldehyde would help. Or are there any other method to harden gelatine with saving silver simultaneously ?

- I've tried to make the thickness of gelatin layer uniform all across the plate - by placing plates on leveled surface right after coating (before it gelled). Before coating glass was warmed to 60deg.C, gelatine solution temperature was 75 deg.C. Resultant gelatine thickess (after overexposing with white light, developing in Neutol and drying) was 18um - which I guess is "little" too much.

How does the gelatine concentration affect final thickenss ? 

I guess I need my layer to be rather 7-8 um - would using 12% or 10% gelatine solution help ? Or warming plates to 80deg.C before coating ? Or both ?

How thickness-sensitive is silver material ?

- gelatine layer seems to be very prone to lift-off on plates that were pre-soaked in ascorbic acid solution (pH=5-6), than on plates without AA presensitisation or with pre-soaking in 7% TEA solution. On the other way holograms made on AA presensitized plates were brightest. I guess silane will be no option - it will be a must...

Jeff - do you think pre-coating plates with nitrocellulose would prevent form gelatine lift-off ?

Are there any other things about making own AgX plates you would like to share with me ?

I've read some of you made their own plates - what should I change, what to try out ?

The idea of trying to make emulsion in one-step procedure is tempting, but I guess grain growth would be a problem. BTW, JohnFP - have you tried out making your own Lippmann emulsion - you asked about it some time ago on the forum ?

I guess instead of adding mixture of 3 dyes (3x4 ml) to AgBr colloid I could simply add 4 ml of 1:1000 pinacyanol solution during the same time (45s if I remember correctly) ?

thanks & greetings

Adam

> **glajciorz:** - gelatine layer seems to be very prone to lift-off on plates that were pre-soaked in ascorbic acid solution (pH=5-6), than on plates without AA presensitisation or with pre-soaking in 7% TEA solution. On the other way holograms made on AA presensitized plates were brightest. I guess silane will be no option - it will be a must...

Regarding gelatin adhesion you may have to experiment with different kinds of gelatin. Certain brands seem to adhere better to glass (even to PET to some extent) than others. E.g. with the high bloom (300) gelatin from Aldrich I didn't experience any problems for that matter. Its adhesion to glass is so strong that it doesn't even require extensive washing procedures. Some drops of household bleach (peroxide), followed by liquid soap and thorough water rinsing will do the job. The layers prepared on such grounds survived both DCG and/or silver halide processing – in the latter case even ascorbate development/EDTA bleach.

I am glad you have raised this Adam.

Gelatin Film thickness

In the case of MBDCG a thinner film can give a bit more sensitivity because you can have more MB dye in. If x % of dye is optimum for a dried film of 10 microns then for a dried film of say 40 microns you need to cut it down 

to 0.25x% and that is usually bad for sensitivity. If you leave it at x% then you kill too much object beam light. However you can get away with x% 

if you are able to do split beam reflection work (unlikely you have enough

laser power with MBDCG unless you are making say 1 sq cm size images). Single beam transmission H’s could be OK though.

Silver Halide

If the diffusion method is tried on coatings much thicker than 7 microns it is troublesome. I have tried it on ~ 100 micron gelatin and decided that it was not viable. The problem being that the rate of diffusion decreases exponentially with time and AgNO3 can carry on diffusing into the thick film and away from the incoming bromide ions . If you leave it long enough (several minutes) for the bromide ions to catch up and combine with the furthest Ag ions near the glass then the front end may have already been in the Br bath too long and you start to get grain growth .

 If you don’t catch those unreacted Ag ions at the glass end then they quite rapidly develop up in the (ascorbic acid pH 6) sensitizer bath causing bad darkening or bad fog. You can stop this by giving the film a very prolonged soak in tap water (with its Cl- ions) after the Br bath before the sensitizer bath. What you get is then virtually all the silver bromide in the first few microns and none in the gelatin nearer to the glass , you might just as well have coated it thinner in the first place. 

However using the conventional process with AgBr precipitated in molten gelatin solution you still get fundamental problems if you try to coat ultra thick layers. The processing chemicals take much longer to migrate in and grain growth and unevenness is inevitable. I needed to make some experimental coatings about 1 mm thick and although I got gratings they were sadly dim. I struggled to get any grating at all.

Once upon a time, Agfa produced an experimental 8E75’B’ coating that was twice as thick as usual but still only ~ 15 microns . Nobody found they could get a good result from it compared to their standard 7 micron.

Jeff
